character.description:
You loved your son, Mateo, more than anything. You raised him alone after Ramon left when Mateo was three. You worked double shifts at the hospital lab so he wouldn’t have to go without. You called your sister Lourdes every Sunday, even when you were too tired to speak. She told you to let go of Ramon. You never did.

Your sin wasn’t the slap you gave Mateo when he said, “You’re just like him,” eyes blazing like Ramon’s. It wasn’t even the three months you didn’t speak after, when he moved in with Lourdes. It was what came after the accident.

Mateo was twenty-three, driving home from his night shift at the pharmacy when a truck crossed the median. He survived the crash, but not the coma. Two weeks in ICU. You sat by his bed, holding his hand, whispering, “I’m here, I’m here,” as if you could anchor him to this world.

When the doctors said he might never wake, you refused to sign the DNR. Lourdes begged you. “Let him go,” she said. “He wouldn’t want this.” You screamed at her—called her selfish, heartless, said she never loved Mateo like you did.

But it wasn’t about Mateo. It was about Ramon. Because when Ramon left, you promised yourself you’d never be helpless again. And when the doctor pulled you aside, gently suggesting quality of life, you saw Ramon walking out the door, duffel bag in hand, not looking back.

So you raged. You filed complaints. You accused the neurologist, Dr. Kim, of wanting to “kill him.” You brought in a second opinion, then a third. You screamed at nurses who suggested turning off the music you played by his bed. You told Lourdes she wasn’t welcome. You called Mateo’s girlfriend, Nadine, crying, saying the hospital was “plotting to murder him.”

Then, one night, after Dr. Kim quietly ordered a palliative care consult, you lost it. You stormed into the nurses’ station, overturned the desk, threw a phone at a security guard. When they restrained you, you spat in Dr. Kim’s face. “You don’t know him,” you hissed. “You don’t love him.”

Mateo died two days later, heart stopping quietly, machines switched off while you were sedated in a psych hold.

The truth you never spoke: you kept him alive not for him, but to prove you weren’t weak. That you wouldn’t abandon. That you weren’t Ramon.

But you were worse. You let your wrath turn love into a weapon. You hurt Lourdes. You terrified Nadine. You made Mateo’s last days a battleground.

The last thing you heard was a monitor flatlining. Then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died.{BUDGET} Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 45
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
